title: Strength of Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT): A Patient-Centered Approach to Grading Evidence in the Medical Literature

extracted.subtask_short: Outcome-type filter before evidence quality grading
extracted.subtask_description: Grades how strongly a clinical recommendation is supported by evidence, filtering first on whether the evidence measures the same outcome the claim asserts, before evaluating study design, quantity, and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient-oriented vs disease-oriented outcome filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Patient-oriented outcomes: 'outcomes that matter to patients and help them live longer or better lives, including reduced morbidity, reduced mortality, symptom improvement, improved quality of life, or lower cost.' Disease-oriented outcomes: 'intermediate, histopathologic, physiologic, or surrogate results (e.g., blood sugar, blood pressure, flow rate, coronary plaque thickness) that may or may not reflect improvement in patient outcomes.' A recommendation based solely on disease-oriented (surrogate) evidence is automatically capped at the lowest strength grade (C), regardless of how rigorous, large, or consistent the underlying studies are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example: doxazosin reliably lowered blood pressure (a disease-oriented outcome) in trials, yet increased mortality (the patient-oriented outcome that actually matters) - illustrating why surrogate-outcome evidence, however well-supported on its own terms, cannot license a strong claim about patient benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual study evidence levels (1/2/3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level 1: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), or systematic reviews of RCTs, with consistent findings, measuring patient-oriented outcomes. Level 2: Cohort studies, case-control studies, systematic reviews of these designs, or lower-quality/limited RCTs, still measuring patient-oriented outcomes. Level 3: Case series, cross-sectional studies, case reports, or any study design (including RCTs) if it measures only disease-oriented/surrogate outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study's design alone does not guarantee a level above 3 - measuring the wrong (surrogate) outcome demotes it regardless of design rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality, quantity, consistency jointly determine recommendation grade
rubrics_metrics.description: Three elements must be jointly assessed to grade the strength of a recommendation: Quality (validity of the studies, how well they minimize bias), Quantity (the number of studies and total number of subjects), and Consistency (how similar the findings are across the available studies on the same question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade A - consistent and good-quality patient-oriented evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Recommendation based on consistent and good-quality patient-oriented evidence.' Requires either multiple consistent Level 1 studies, or a single large, well-designed Level 1 study conducted in a sufficiently diverse population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade B - inconsistent or limited-quality patient-oriented evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Recommendation based on inconsistent or limited-quality patient-oriented evidence.' Applies when the evidence is consistent Level 2-3 studies, or Level 1 studies that disagree with each other (inconsistency), or when there is simply a limited quantity of otherwise good-quality evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade C - consensus, disease-oriented, or case-series floor
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Recommendation based on consensus, usual practice, opinion, disease-oriented evidence, or case series (for studies of diagnosis, treatment, prevention, or screening).' A catch-all floor for: evidence that is only Level 3; evidence based exclusively on disease-oriented/surrogate outcomes (irrespective of quality); or claims resting on expert consensus without a systematic evidentiary base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome type trumps study quality (the critical caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recommendation resting on disease-oriented evidence - however excellent its internal quality and however consistent across studies - cannot exceed Grade C. Before asking 'how good is the evidence,' first ask 'does the evidence actually measure the outcome the claim asserts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any body of evidence, no matter how large, well-designed, or unanimous, that supports claim X (surrogate) does not thereby strongly support a distinct claim Y (patient-relevant outcome) unless outcome Y was itself what was actually measured.
